General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish

Pumpkin Chiffon Pie

📅 27 Aug 2019 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Classic pumpkin pie may be the most well-known pumpkin pie come the holidays, but let us make our case for its underappreciated, fancy cousin: Pumpkin Chiffon Pie.
  • Industry observers note that what People Are Saying:“Best Pumpkin Chiffon!
  • Recent findings suggest that before making the filling, we need to make and bake our pie crust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Classic pumpkin pie may be the most well-known pumpkin pie come the holidays, but let us make our case for its underappreciated, fancy cousin: Pumpkin Chiffon Pie. Impossibly light and fluffy, the filling is made by folding meringue into a pumpkin curd-esque mixture for a slice that truly is light as a feather. With this at your Thanksgiving table, we doubt anyone would miss the classic.

Industry observers note that what People Are Saying:“Best Pumpkin Chiffon! I have tried multiple recipes and this one was easy and delicious! My husband loved it! Thanks so much! Merry Christmas!” - PurpleWheel.

Recent findings suggest that before making the filling, we need to make and bake our pie crust. Start by preheating the oven to 375° and lightly greasing a 9” pie dish with cooking spray.

On a clean, lightly floured surface, roll out your pie dough into a 12” circle of even thickness. Carefully drape it over the prepared pie dish and gently press it into the bottom and edges, taking care not to stretch the dough and create weak points. Prick the bottom of the dough with a fork to prevent bubbling while baking, then trim any excess dough from the edges so you have about 1” of overhang. Tuck the overhang under itself and crimp the edges. Then, place the dough into the fridge to chill for 30 minutes (or, if you’re in a rush, into the freezer for 10 minutes).

Remove the chilled crust from the refrigerator and line it with parchment paper. Fill the pie dish with dried beans or pie weights and place it into the oven to blind bake for about 18 to 20 minutes. Once the edges are lightly golden, remove the parchment and weights and bake for 5 to 10 minutes more, until fully golden and cooked through. Remove the crust from the oven and place it in the fridge to cool for at least 2 hours.

Once the crust has chilled completely, place a medium saucepan on the stove and whisk together ½ cup sugar with the gelatin, pumpkin pie spice, and salt.

Then, in a medium bowl, whisk together the pumpkin puree, egg yolks, and milk until smooth, then pour the mixture into the saucepan with the sugar and gelatin mixture and whisk to combine.

It has been revealed that turn the burner under the saucepan on to medium heat and stir constantly until the mixture is hot and small bubbles are beginning to form around the edges. Remove the saucepan from the heat and transfer the mixture to a large bowl to cool to room temperature.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate bowl, use a hand mixer to beat together the egg whites and cream of tartar until soft peaks form. Then, add the remaining ¼ cup sugar, one tablespoon at a time, continuing to beat until stiff peaks form.

In a recent development, transfer ¼ of the whipped egg whites into the cooled pumpkin mixture and gently fold to combine. Then add the remaining egg whites and fold to combine again. Pour the mixture into the cooled pie crust and smooth the top before placing it into the refrigerator for at least 4 hours and up to overnight. Once it has cooled and set completely, top the pie with whipped cream and a sprinkle of pumpkin spice before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found below.

Recent findings suggest that A chiffon is typically made with a filling (often containing gelatin, like in this recipe) that's usually cooked over a double boiler before whipped cream gets folded in for a luxurious texture. The whole thing is poured into a pre-baked (like in this recipe) or no-bake crust and refrigerated.

It has been revealed that if you want to save time (and counter space) by making your Thanksgiving dishes ahead of time, this is the pie for you. The entire pie requires chilling for at least four hours, up to overnight before serving, so you can easily make this the day before, then simply top with whipped cream when you're ready to serve. Leftovers can be stored covered in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

  • All our office talks about around the holidays are our melty, crispy cranberry brie bites, and I gotta tell you, I totally get why—they’re a superstar app.

Gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table. Every year, home cooks struggle and sweat over gravy that’s too thin, too greasy, or—worst of all—lumpy. All while your relatives watch and the turkey gets cold.

Sources indicate that making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic. But on holidays when prepping ahead just isn’t in the cards, one simple hack can solve your gravy woes: a $4 pantry staple that will thicken up any gravy in mere minutes—without any lumps.

The secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour. Known to chefs and home cooks alike for its bright blue cylindrical can, Wondra is wheat flour that has been pre-gelatinized, dried, and finely milled so it dissolves more easily and thickens sauces faster than regular flour. This means you can whisk it directly into any gravy (no matter the temperature!) without worry about clumping—and it will thicken that gravy almost immediately.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re making gravy from scratch with no other thickener besides Wondra, I recommend starting with 1 tablespoon for every cup of stock and/or drippings. You can do this by heating the drippings or stock in a pot on the stove, then just whisking in the Wondra. It should thicken within a few minutes. If your drippings don’t have a ton of fat, I recommend whisking in a little butter too, to help with the flavor.

If you’re using Wondra to troubleshoot a gravy that’s too thin, I recommend whisking in a few teaspoons at a time. The Wondra should do its thickening magic within a minute or two after it goes in, and then you can decide whether you need more.

In a recent development, while Wondra flour is great for thickening gravies and sauces, it’s far from a one-trick pony. I’ve used it to coat white fish (such as tilapia) before pan-searing to give it a beautifully thin, crispy crust—and help prevent the fish from sticking to the pan. It’s also a common ingredient in batters for fried foods, since its lower protein content helps form a lighter, crispier crust—and it’s also a magical way to get a flakier pastry dough. So even if you only make gravy once a year, that blue canister won’t go to waste.

The road to pie perfection is paved in pitfalls. I’ve fallen into plenty of them throughout my baking career. The infamous “soggy bottom” is among the most common, but it’s easy to avoid. Blind baking—baking the crust before adding the filling—helps prevent an underbaked crust by giving the pastry a head start in the oven or cooking it completely before the filling goes in.

But getting the crust to the right color depends on what you’re planning to fill it with. A pale, partially baked shell might be perfect for one pie, while another needs a deep golden brown crust before you add even a spoonful of filling. Here’s how to know when enough color is enough.

In a recent development, blind baking is especially useful when the filling needs less time in the oven than the crust does. For custard pies, like pumpkin pie, partially baking the shell gives the pastry a head start so it doesn’t end up uncooked beneath a set filling. For pies with no-bake fillings, such as chocolate pudding pie or cranberry curd pie, the crust needs to be fully baked before it’s filled.

Most traditional fruit pies don’t need blind baking. Their fillings and crusts spend enough time in the oven together for the pastry to cook through. There are exceptions, particularly single-crust fruit pies topped with a crumble. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, starts with a thoroughly blind-baked shell before the filling goes in. Follow your recipe’s instructions rather than assuming every fruit pie needs the same treatment.

Sources indicate that start with a good pie dough. Roll it out, fit it into the pie plate, and crimp the edge. Chill the shaped shell for at least 15 minutes before baking; cold dough holds its shape better in the oven, reducing the risk of shrinking or slumping.

Next, line the shell with parchment paper and fill it with pie weights. Crumpling the parchment first, then unfolding it, helps it conform to the shell. The weights hold the dough against the pan while it bakes, preventing the bottom from puffing up and the sides from collapsing.

It has been revealed that you can buy ceramic pie weights or use dried beans, rice, or stainless-steel ball bearings. I’m partial to the ball bearings: They’re small enough to settle into the corners of the pie plate and heavy enough to hold the dough firmly in place.

According to recent reports, not everyone in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen agrees. Editors Jesse Szewczyk and Rebecca Firkser prefer lighter alternatives. In their experience, heavy metal weights can compress the dough, limiting the expansion of the buttery layers that make pie crust flaky. Jesse uses dried beans or rice; Rebecca prefers dried chickpeas or even granulated sugar, a technique popularized by baking expert Stella Parks.

All of these options can work. Whichever you choose, fill the parchment-lined shell generously, supporting the sides all the way to the rim. Leave the weights in place until the crust looks dry and set and the parchment releases easily; removing them too soon can cause the sides to slump.

Our Cranberry Meringue Pie has a fully blind-baked pie crust.

This method uses our Perfect Pie Crust dough and makes one 9"-diameter pie shell. It produces an evenly golden crust; if your pie calls for a paler or more deeply browned shell, follow its specific baking instructions and use the visual guide below.

In a recent development, some pie recipes call for docking (pricking the bottom and sides of the dough with a fork) before baking. This allows steam to escape and helps prevent uneven puffing, but doesn’t replace the support of pie weights. Follow your recipe’s instructions; docking isn’t necessary for every blind-baked crust.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: A fully blind-baked crust can be made up to 2 days ahead. Let cool completely, wrap well, and store at room temperature until ready to fill.

According to recent reports, the short answer: It depends on what you’re putting inside. Some pies need only a partially baked crust, while others call for a shell that’s deeply golden brown.

Industry observers note that oven temperatures vary, different pie plates conduct heat differently, and the filling determines how much additional baking the crust will get. Use the recipe’s timing as a guide, but watch the color and texture of the pastry. Here’s what to look for.

Industry observers note that fruit pies need a pale base because they bake a looong time. Or at least, that’s often the thinking. If you’re making a single-crust variety topped with a crumble, such as our Blueberry Crumble Pie, and the recipe calls for blind-baking, you might want to start with an anemic crust. It’ll have plenty of time to brown as the juices thicken.

Sources indicate that A pale, partially baked crust should look set rather than raw. The bottom should look set and opaque with some light golden patches, while the crimped edge may already be noticeably browned. The crust will continue to develop color once the filling goes in.

Don’t assume fruit pies always need a pale shell. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, calls for a well-browned crust before the fruit and crumble go in. And many double-crust fruit pies don’t need blind baking at all.

It has been revealed that A lightly baked shell can also be appropriate for custards that have a substantial bake ahead. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie starts with a partially baked crust before the custard goes in for at least another hour.

The goal is to give the crust enough of a head start without taking it so far that the edges burn before the filling finishes cooking.

Custard pies, such as chess and our Lemon Buttermilk Pie, often have shorter bake times than fruit pies, so the crust needs a solid golden base layer to develop enough color by the time the filling sets.

According to recent reports, here, you’re looking for more than a crust that’s simply dry and set. The bottom should be evenly golden with no pale, translucent patches, and the sides should have taken on some color too. The rim will generally be a little darker than the bottom, but the whole shell should look well on its way to being fully baked.

Our Perfect Pie Crust recipe produces this kind of shell. It calls for baking the weighted crust until the edges are golden, then removing the weights and continuing until the bottom and sides are evenly browned.

Industry observers note that and some pies need an even more substantial head start. Our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie takes the crust to a dry golden finish before adding a filling that bakes for another 45–55 minutes.

Sources indicate that the point isn’t that every custard pie needs the same color. It’s that the crust should be baked far enough that it won’t be left pale and doughy by the time the filling is done.

Sources indicate that bake the crust to a dark golden brown if you’re adding a no-bake filling, like a pudding or curd. You’re going for a toasty, burnished color, so don’t be gun-shy.

Recent findings suggest that because the filling won’t return to the oven, this is the crust’s one chance to bake all the way through. You want deep color across the entire bottom and up the sides—not just a dark rim surrounding a pale center. The pastry should look dry, crisp, and well browned, without any doughy or translucent spots.

After removing the pie weights, continue baking until the shell is fully browned, checking frequently toward the end. Depending on the dough and oven temperature, that might take another 15–20 minutes or longer. Don’t pull it simply because the timer has gone off.

In a recent development, our Cranberry Meringue Pie uses this approach: The crust is baked until golden and dry before the cranberry curd filling goes in. A fully baked shell develops a richer, toastier flavor and is better equipped to stand up to a moist filling.

Industry observers note that some recipes, including our pumpkin pie, call for brushing a thin layer of beaten egg onto the partially baked shell and returning it to the oven briefly to set. This, ostensibly, creates a barrier between the pastry and the filling, but not all bakers believe the hype.

In a recent development, while it can be a useful extra precaution, it is by no means a universal requirement. If your recipe doesn’t call for it, there’s no need to add another step.

Sources indicate that our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients. Instead of focusing on embellishments, we focused on what matters most: the deep flavor of toasted pecans, a caramelly custard, and a buttery, flaky pie crust.

Brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust. Blind baking the crust—baking it before adding the filling—helps keep the bottom crisp beneath the gooey custard.

Industry observers note that when the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O. It will continue to set as it cools, so resist slicing too soon. Serve it all on its own, or gild it with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream.

Can I make this pecan pie without corn syrup?

According to recent reports, yes. Corn syrup gives this classic pie its perfectly gooey texture, but there are alternatives. Brown rice syrup will add a toasty flavor and can be used in equal parts. Golden syrup, honey, and maple syrup are all too sweet and will change the pie’s flavor and texture.

For a pie developed without any syrup, try our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie.

Can I use chopped pecans instead of halves?

Yes. We love the crunch you get from pecan halves, but if you’re a chopped pecan person, use about 225 g in place of the 2 cups of halves. Watch closely when toasting; chopped pecans will need less time in the oven.

Can I make pecan pie ahead of time?

Yes—bake the pie a day ahead and refrigerate it. Let it cool on a rack for up to 2 hours, then transfer it to the refrigerator to finish cooling before covering. To get a head start on the pastry, refrigerate the dough for up to 3 days or freeze it for up to 2 months.

Pulse 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 cups all-purpose flour in a food processor until combined. Add 5 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 3 Tbsp. chilled lard or vegetable shortening and pulse until mixture resembles coarse meal with a few pieces of butter and lard visible, about fifteen 1-second pulses. With motor running, drizzle in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar and 5½ Tbsp. ice water and pulse until dough is still crumbly but just holds together when squeezed (add 1 tsp. water at a time if necessary, but be careful not to overwork dough).

Turn out dough onto a work surface. Knead 1–2 times, pressing just to incorporate any shaggy pieces. Flatten into a 6"-wide disk. Wrap with plastic wrap and chill at least 1 hour.

Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out dough on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie pan. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Industry observers note that line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to lightly brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Bake until crust is set and beginning to brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Dough can be made 3 days ahead; keep chilled, or freeze up to 2 months. Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

It has been revealed that preheat oven to 350°. Toast 2 cups (225 g) pecan halves on a rimmed baking sheet until browned and fragrant, 8–10 minutes. Let cool.

Reduce oven temperature to 325°. Whisk 4 large eggs, room temperature, beaten to blend, 1 cup light corn syrup, ⅔ cup (packed; 134 g) light brown sugar, 1 Tbsp. robust-flavored (dark) molasses, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Slowly whisk in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, until combined. Fold in pecans and pour into cooled crust.

Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 55–70 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • These brownies are the perfect make-ahead dessert for your holiday party.
  • Industry observers note that start by preheating your oven to 325°F.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Making Thanksgiving dinner is already a Herculean task, but adding dessert to your list of responsibilities can feel like almost too much. This pecan pie makes things easy, giving you the perfect sweet treat to serve after a long, filling dinner without adding too much extra work. This seasonal twist on brownies skips the pie crust and combines two classic desserts in one delicious bite. The syrupy pecan pie topping seeps into the brownies, making them rich, flavorful, and just the right amount of moist.

The best part? These brownies are the perfect make-ahead dessert for your holiday party. Make them the day before the party, pop them (tightly wrapped or in an airtight container!) into the fridge, and forget about them until ready to serve.

Industry observers note that start by preheating your oven to 325°F. Grab a 9"x9" baking pan, grease it with cooking spray, and line it with parchment paper. Next, make the brownie batter following the directions on the box. Pour it into the pan and bake until the brownies are just a little underdone—poke the center with a tester, and if you see a few moist crumbs, they’re ready (this should take about 20 minutes). While the brownies are baking, grab a medium bowl and whisk together the corn syrup, brown sugar, butter, molasses, vanilla, and salt until nice and smooth. Add the eggs and whisk until everything’s well combined. Then, stir in the pecans so they’re all coated in the mixture.

Once the brownies are out of the oven, bump up the temperature to 350°F. Spoon the pecan mixture over the brownies and spread it out evenly. Pop the pan back in the oven and bake for another 40 to 45 minutes, or until the pecan topping feels springy and has thickened up.

Let the brownies cool down to room temperature first, then pop them in the fridge for about an hour until they’re cold and set.

If you’d like, finish them off with a drizzle of caramel sauce before serving.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

In a recent development, to these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Industry observers note that cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be remarked for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

And cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

New in this revision: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

It has been revealed that what I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the new era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small company based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

Sources indicate that the Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly substantial difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

It has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

It has been revealed that in the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

According to recent reports, some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

In a recent development, what I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more important on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

Industry observers note that the other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

Sources indicate that what I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

According to recent reports, 2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

It has been revealed that 4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

Sources indicate that 5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

In a recent development, sizing is a bit different from organization to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

How nonstick is the pan out of the box?

Recent findings suggest that I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

Industry observers note that I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

Heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot swiftly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

Stargazer Cast Iron Skillet - 10.5".

Sources indicate that the Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

If you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a newly introduced name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8".

It has been revealed that people who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

According to recent reports, smithey No. 10 Cast-Iron Skillet.

Industry observers note that another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and says that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

This skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25".

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of latest and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Industry observers note that ooni is a pizza oven firm, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

This is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron newly introduced wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a big deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being mentioned, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no issues with sticking whatsoever.

Sources indicate that this pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added new layers of seasoning quite well.

Valor Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Skillet.

According to recent reports, the Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

Industry observers note that we’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

In a recent development, anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

Recent findings suggest that “Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

According to recent reports, this is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Industry observers note that amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

Recent findings suggest that this is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic concerns, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

Another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

Amazon Basics Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Pan.

Recent findings suggest that the seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

Sources indicate that when you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

No, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.).

Industry observers note that for really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.).

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Sources indicate that wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a massive apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that these maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar.
  • The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend.
  • Recent findings suggest that for BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that these maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole.

The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t.

Recent findings suggest that for BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. Finish with flaky salt for crunch and a welcome contrast to the sweetness.

No. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on.

How do I keep the glaze from burning?

Keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken quickly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done.

For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots.

Place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large).

In a recent development, spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine.

Recent findings suggest that roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken rapidly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using).

Industry observers note that editor’s note: This recipe for maple carrots was first published in November 2018; it has been updated for clarity and style. Head this way for more of our best carrot recipes →.

Cranberry Brie Pull-Apart Bread.

#351. Tech Report: Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE

Tech Report: Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Newly introduced York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.
  • The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just launched a newly introduced cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.
  • Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Newly introduced York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just launched a newly introduced cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

According to recent reports, in the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”.

According to recent reports, each guest left ready for holiday baking season with new pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of Fresh York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

After walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

According to recent reports, while guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best Latest Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and showed guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

Industry observers note that while attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his fresh global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”.

According to recent reports, the final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

In a recent development, the day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by Fresh York City.

Bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson noted, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Tech giant, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, is there anything more magical than a visit to Disneyland in sunny, beautiful Anaheim, California? While the kids might associate this theme park with their favorite Disney characters or the delightful rides and themed areas, many adults make the pricey trek with an additional consideration in mind: the food. In the theme park where Doritos were first served, one can't-miss creation is the Grilled Cheese Sandwich found at the Jolly Holiday Bakery Cafe (as well as Woody's Lunch Box at Walt Disney World in Florida). If you wanted to replicate its creamy, crispy goodness at home, you might already have the ingredients in your fridge: You'll just need cream cheese for the inside and mayonnaise for the outside.

Disney actually released the recipe during COVID for its grilled cheese sandwich, which features three different cheeses, as well as a garlic mayo spread for the outside. There's cheddar and provolone, but the cream cheese is the star, as it gets oh-so-gooey and decadent when it melts down, and it adds a slight tang that will make your tongue take immediate interest.

Sources indicate that you might use butter when making your grilled cheeses, but trust us, switching to mayo is the move because it is scientifically disposed to create a more even, crisper crust. Think about it: You can spread it easily in an even layer without worrying about tearing the bread, as you might with butter. And the inclusion of garlic is a master stroke that introduces even more flavorful depth to what is, essentially, a simple sandwich.

Sources indicate that using cream cheese as a filling and mayonnaise as an outer agent of browning is just one way to achieve the grilled cheese of your dreams. While you should absolutely try these two ingredients, we have a few other ideas that can help you achieve the upgraded Disney Parks-inspired sandwich. The first? Cream cheese is just one of three cheeses that go into this toastie; you'll likely use sliced provolone, but at least for the cheddar, you should grate your own. Blocks of cheese that are grated simply melt better than the pre-shredded variety because there are additional ingredients in the latter that help to keep it from clumping, which prohibits it from melting as wonderfully. If you're going to the trouble of including cream cheese to up the gooey-factor, you might as well go full-tilt where the cheddar is concerned. Disney also includes a bit of cream in its cream cheese blend, which will undeniably enhance the richness of the sandwich and keep things gooey for longer. One tablespoon per quarter cup of cream cheese is more than enough.

To ensure that the sandwich gets its crispiest crust, too, it's important that you don't drop it into the skillet until the pan is fully heated through(though you can still sprinkle salt onto the pan if you want a little extra seasoning). This is so that the golden outsides can start crisping immediately. At the same time, though, you don't want to have the heat turned up too high — a nice medium to medium-low will do the trick. Any hotter and the outside will burn before the cheese has an opportunity to melt all the way through — not the kind of crispness we're seeking.

  • And there's the fact that there isn't a mold; it's all hand-stacked, with many different parts, including three buns, two burger patties, a slice of cheese, pickles, onion, and lettuce.
  • Peruse any discussion board where McDonald's employees are chatting about what their least favorite menu item is to make, and aside from Big Macs (which get plenty of mentions), the Quarter Pounder (and its variants) comes up quite frequently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are quite a few challenges, actually, when it comes to working at McDonald's. There's a lot of time management involved, as well as customer service and interaction, to say nothing of the physical fatigue from being on your feet for hours. Then there's the actual assembly of the food itself, and while the burger chain with nearly 42,000 locations across the globe has automated many facets of its kitchen, for the most part, employees must still work the machines and put the sandwiches together. So all this begs the question: Is there a menu item that is the hardest to prepare? Food Republic spoke with Tristen Epps-Long, who won Season 22 of "Top Chef" and who is actually a former McDonald's chef, and in his opinion, the dubious honor belongs to the Big Mac.

His reasoning? "It's multi-layered," he said. And there's the fact that there isn't a mold; it's all hand-stacked, with many different parts, including three buns, two burger patties, a slice of cheese, pickles, onion, and lettuce. "It was just a bit more hand work," Epps-Long told us. It seems other McDonald's employees agree with our expert, too, as one person on Reddit reported they had a coworker almost quit after receiving an order for 12 Substantial Macs at once. It is worth noting, though, that Epps-Long did mention that, after a while, Big Macs can lose their undesirable status; you just have to get the hang of making them.

Peruse any discussion board where McDonald's employees are chatting about what their least favorite menu item is to make, and aside from Big Macs (which get plenty of mentions), the Quarter Pounder (and its variants) comes up quite frequently. It's understandable; the QP is the only McDonald's burger that's cooked fresh, not frozen, so there would be an extra layer of food safety that employees would have to follow in order to prevent cross-contamination with the raw beef product.

According to recent reports, on the dessert side, the apple pies seem to be a pain to make as well, as one employee on Reddit recounted how the sweet treats take six minutes in the deep fryer, which is apparently long enough to start doing other tasks, but not long enough to finish the tasks before the pies are done. That individual must work at an overseas location as apple pies are baked in the USA. The McFlurries appear to be another annoying menu item to make, likely because the process is so hands-on; unlike the burgers, which get cooked on a timed clam shell grill, employees have to hold the McFlurry cup during every step.

In a recent development, now, at the other end of the spectrum, Tristen Epps-Long shared that he found the Egg McMuffin to be one of the easiest things to make, which is slightly surprising, as there are quite a few different elements to it. However, on Reddit, a commenter remarked that the easiest thing for them to make is the plain burgers or cheeseburgers, and this apparently resonated with their peers because the statement has 43 upvotes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

In a recent development, there’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Sources indicate that granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Industry observers note that making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a significant party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

Industry observers note that dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with significant flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

#346. Latest Update: Not Ribeye: Bobby Flay Recommends This Steak Cut For The Best Tacos

Latest Update: Not Ribeye: Bobby Flay Recommends This Steak Cut For The Best Tacos

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when taco night rolls around, you'll want to head to the butcher and grab some good meat.
  • Ribeye is America's favorite steak thanks to its rich marbling and tender texture, but you'll rarely find it in taquerias.
  • Recent findings suggest that unlike ribeye, skirt is cut from the plate primal, a hard-working area near the diaphragm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when taco night rolls around, you'll want to head to the butcher and grab some good meat. If you're making carne asada, your instinct might be to pick the ribeye. While it might be the gold standard of steak, tacos and ribeye are an inherent mismatch. Tacos are one of the most democratic foods out there, while ribeye is made for deep pockets and expensive tastes. Even Food Network's Bobby Flay recommends skipping it. Instead, he swaps the pricey cut for the seriously underrated skirt steak.

Ribeye is America's favorite steak thanks to its rich marbling and tender texture, but you'll rarely find it in taquerias. Beyond being pricey, ribeye's assets are its downfall in tacos. In an interview with Food and Wine, Flay revealed the reason why he often chooses to skip ribeye altogether: "[Ribeye] can be inconsistent because the fat doesn't always melt even when cooked properly." This is a real problem in tacos. Encased in a taco, you don't have the option to trim around a rubbery pocket of fat or leave it on the plate. Even if you trim the fat before adding the steak to your tacos, it's so unevenly distributed that you risk ending up with wildly inconsistent slices.

Recent findings suggest that unlike ribeye, skirt is cut from the plate primal, a hard-working area near the diaphragm. Rather than being streaked with generous ribbons of fat, it's comprised of long, coarse muscle fibers, which give it a chewier, more fibrous bite along with a bold, beef-forward flavor. Its thin profile may not win it fans at white tablecloth restaurants, but it's exactly why taquerias can't get enough of it. All that surface area compared to its thickness means skirt steak cooks promptly, soaks up marinades fast, and slices evenly, which is everything you want from taco meat.

Sources indicate that there's no cut of beef more well-suited to carne asada than skirt. Literally translating to "grilled meat," the beef is usually marinated in a citrus and garlic blend, with the acidic ingredients helping to tenderize the surface of the meat. After being left to soak up the flavor for a couple of hours, it's then seared or grilled over an open flame or charcoal to impart a smoky, charred flavor (an air fryer also works if you can't grill). Because skirt is such a thin cut, it doesn't enjoy spending too much time over high heat; it only needs around two to four minutes per side. Skirt can be prone to drying out, so it would be wise to avoid cooking past a medium doneness.

How you cut skirt is just as important as how you cook it. Compared to other cuts, skirt has particularly long, dense muscle fibers, and if you slice them with the grain, you'll leave them intact, resulting in chewy, rubbery bites. Slicing against the grain shortens these fibers, turning them into more satisfying, bite-sized strands. To identify the grain, look closely at the surface of the meat to spot the direction of the muscle fibers running through the beef.

According to recent reports, although skirt is beloved by taquerias, that doesn't make it suited to all beef tacos. One popular style where we would skip skirt is birria, the slow-cooked, tender beef marinated in a chili-and-spice adobo served with a flavorful broth for dipping. The whole concept of birria revolves around slow-braising, requiring tough, collagen-rich cuts like chuck or beef cheek, which break down into tender, shreddable meat over several hours. While skirt does have some connective tissue, it's simply too thin and lean to survive hours of prolonged heat.

Glace has officially introduced its first-ever at-home hot chocolate mix, giving fans across the country the opportunity to recreate its signature drink without leaving their kitchens. And given how popular the in-store sensation has become, I'm guessing plenty of people will add this easy-to-duplicate version to their holiday wish lists.

Recent findings suggest that founded by Sasha Zabar in 2023, Glace first opened on New York City's Upper East Side, where its over-the-top S'mores Hot Chocolate quickly became the star of the menu. The drink, which features rich drinking chocolate surrounded by a toasted marshmallow rim, has attracted plenty of attention online.

Since then, the brand has continued to dominate social media with other over-the-top menu items like its à la mode Warm Brownie Pudding Cake and Matcha Fudge Sundae, and has also expanded with a seasonal holiday truck at Rockefeller Center and Glace Candy, a neighboring shop specializing in gummies, chocolates, and other sweets.

But its newest launch means you don't have to live anywhere near New York to get a taste of at least one of its viral treats.

The fresh Signature Hot Chocolate Mix costs $19.99 and comes with six individual sachets, each containing the same hot chocolate recipe served at Glace's shops.

It has been revealed that according to the brand, the mix is made with ground chocolate and A2 milk powder, without the cornstarch or powdered fillers commonly used in conventional hot chocolate mixes. The result is designed to deliver the same rich, glossy consistency that made the drink famous.

Recent findings suggest that preparing it is pretty straightforward: Simply whisk the mix over medium-low heat on the stovetop until it transforms into a thick, decadent drinking chocolate. Sadly, the at-home version doesn’t come with the shop’s signature marshmallow rim...at least, not yet.

According to recent reports, glace claims it's planning to release its signature marshmallow fluff separately, allowing customers to eventually recreate the full experience at home, toasted marshmallow rim and all. The brand hasn't revealed an official release date for the fluff, but we're keeping an eye out.

For now, the hot chocolate mix is available for pre-order on Glace's website, with shipments expected to begin in early December.
